mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a permutation and a combination?

acceptedAnswer.text: A permutation counts ordered arrangements, so (1, 2, 3) and (3, 2, 1) are different. A combination counts unordered selections, so they are the same. Because each combination of size r can be arranged in r! ways, the number of permutations is always r! times the number of combinations.

mainEntity.name: Why is a “combination lock” really a permutation lock?

acceptedAnswer.text: Because the order in which you enter the digits matters: 1-2-3 opens it but 3-2-1 does not. Strictly it is a count of ordered sequences, so it uses permutation formulas (with repetition if digits can be reused).

mainEntity.name: How does this calculator handle very large factorials?

acceptedAnswer.text: It uses arbitrary-precision integer arithmetic, so results are exact rather than rounded to floating-point. Numbers with more than 18 digits are shown in scientific notation, and “Copy exact value” copies every digit.

It is a method for counting combinations with repetition. Choosing r items from n types, with repeats allowed and order ignored, is equivalent to placing r stars and n − 1 bars in a row, which gives C(n + r − 1, r).

mainEntity.name: What is 0! and what if r = 0?

acceptedAnswer.text: By definition 0! = 1. Choosing zero items can be done in exactly one way, so C(n, 0) = P(n, 0) = 1, and n⁰ = 1.

mainEntity.name: Why can r not exceed n without repetition?

acceptedAnswer.text: You cannot pick more distinct items than exist, so the count is 0. The calculator asks you to enter r ≤ n for the no-repetition formulas; with repetition allowed, r may be larger than n.
